papers.title_in_file: Wasserstein Distances on Quantum Structures: an Overview
papers.what_it_is: A review of quantum generalisations of Wasserstein (optimal transport) distances between quantum states, with open problems.

assertions.value: The authors state that each current definition of a quantum Wasserstein distance gives up one property in return for satisfying the rest, so no single 'true' generalisation exists yet.
quotes: Each of the current definitions has chosen something to sacrifice
in return for a definition which satisfies the rest of the properties.
assertions.certainty_reason: Review authors' survey statement of the state of the field.

assertions.value: The authors report that a qWGAN built on the W1H norm of De Palma et al. retains high gradients as the number of qubits increases, which addresses barren plateaus in quantum GANs.
quotes: The advantage of this is that it retains high gradients even as the number of qubits increases, effectively tackling the issue of barren plateaus.
assertions.certainty_reason: Result attributed to other work; the review runs no experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum Wasserstein GAN models have succeeded only on toy examples and that wider implementation is needed for practical use.
quotes: While some models have had success with toy examples, wider implementation is needed for practical use.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own statement of a limit of the field, Section 9.

papers.title_in_file: AltGraph: Redesigning Quantum Circuits Using Generative Graph Models for Efficient Optimization
papers.what_it_is: Proposes generative graph models (D-VAE and DeepGMG variants) that produce equivalent, smaller quantum circuits from circuit DAGs.

assertions.value: The authors report that AltGraph reduces the gate count by 37.55% on average and the circuit depth by 37.75% after transpiling, with a mean squared error of 0.0074 in the density matrix.
quotes: AltGraph achieves on average a 37.55% reduction in the number of gates and a 37.75% reduction in the circuit depth post-transpiling compared to the original transpiled circuit with only 0.0074 Mean Squared Error (MSE) in the density matrix.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single study, simulated circuits.
assertions.reader_inference: The figures are for the GRU variant per the Conclusions.

assertions.value: The authors state that original and reconstructed circuits were transpiled with Qiskit's FakeWashingtonV2 to emulate hardware.
quotes: both the reconstructed and original circuits are transpiled using Qiskit's FakeWashingtonV2 to emulate performance on cutting-edge hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' statement of their evaluation setup, Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors state that mean squared error has drawbacks as an evaluation metric and that its link to functional accuracy of the circuit needs a deeper probe.
quotes: Despite the models exhibiting robust learning capabilities, using MSELoss as an evaluative metric has its drawbacks.
A deeper probe into the relationship between a low MSELoss and a model's functional accuracy is warranted.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' stated limit, Section 5.2.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum machine learning of graph-structured data
papers.what_it_is: Describes training of quantum neural networks on quantum states attached to graph vertices, using the graph edges to improve learning.

assertions.value: The authors report from simulated pilot studies that the network performs better in testing when the graph structure is used during training.
quotes: One can easily observe that the network performs better during the testing procedure: see Fig. 4b, where the graph structure was exploited during training.
assertions.certainty_reason: Small exact-simulation pilot; one example shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that the simulations were exact classical simulations and were limited to small quantum systems.
quotes: These pilot studies were carried out using an exact simulation of the quantum systems on a classical computer.
Due to the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space dimension with qubit number, we were limited to small quantum systems.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' statement of scope, Section V.

assertions.value: The authors claim that scalable quantum implementations of the learning procedures are likely feasible on the next generation of quantum devices.
quotes: Scalable quantum implementations of the learning procedures are likely feasible on the next generation of quantum computing devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: Forward-looking claim without evidence in the paper.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, and a scan of propositions and theorem statements.
papers.what_it_is: A mathematics paper on noncommutative (quantum) Riemannian geometry and geodesic flows on graphs.
papers.why_not: Pure noncommutative differential geometry on graphs; no machine learning, no computing workload, no finance, policy or evaluation method.

papers.title_in_file: Improving VQE Parameter Quality on Noisy Quantum Processors with Cost-Effective Readout Error Mitigation
papers.what_it_is: Hardware study of VQE for small molecules showing readout error mitigation (T-REx) on an old 5-qubit IBM device beats an unmitigated 156-qubit device.

assertions.value: The authors report that a 5-qubit IBMQ Belem with T-REx gave ground-state energy estimates an order of magnitude more accurate than a 156-qubit IBM Fez without error mitigation, for small molecular systems.
quotes: 5-qubit quantum processing unit (IBMQ Belem), when combined with optimized Twirled Readout Error Extinction (T-REx), achieves ground-state energy estimations an order of magnitude more accurate than those obtained from a more advanced 156-qubit device (IBM Fez) without error mitigation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study, small molecules.

assertions.value: The authors state that only a single VQE run was made on each quantum computer because of cost limitations.
quotes: although we have only considered a single VQE for each quantum computer due to cost limitations
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' stated limit, Section V.

assertions.value: The authors suggest that the simpler T-REx method gave a better QPU result than ZNE, likely because non-negligible coherent noise hindered ZNE.
quotes: the simpler T-REx mitigation method still produced a better QPU result. This is likely due to the presence of non-negligible coherent noise, which hindered ZNE from achieving better results.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors give this as a likely explanation, not a tested one.

papers.title_in_file: A Comparison of Quadratic and Higher-Order Representations for QAOA
papers.what_it_is: Compares QUBO and HUBO formulations of a routing problem under QAOA, in simulation and on IBM hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report that the higher-order (HUBO) form gave better solution quality and better qubit scaling than the quadratic (QUBO) form, but required more two-qubit gates.
quotes: We find that the higher-order form yields better solution quality and scales better in terms of numbers of qubits, but requires more two-qubit gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Small test cases of one routing problem.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the largest test case the HUBO circuits had roughly 6x the depth of the QUBO circuits, and factoring reduced this to around 4x.
quotes: In the worst case of the largest test case, the HUBO generated circuits that had roughly 6x the depth of the QUBO circuits, while the factoring improved this to around 4x.
assertions.certainty_reason: Four small test cases, one problem.

assertions.value: The authors state that the full example is infeasible on current devices, so small test cases were run with 1 QAOA layer, 1024 shots and ten repeats, with hardware runs on the 156 qubit IBM Fez.
quotes: Consequently, the example provided in Figure 3 is infeasible to be run on the currently available quantum devices.
The number of layers, p was fixed at 1 to minimise the impact due to noise.
each run of QAOA was performed for 1024 shots.
each test case was repeated ten times to provide averages for each metric
Experimentation on real hardware was performed on the 156 qubit IBM Fez device.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' statement of experimental setup, Section 4.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Wiener architecture for quantum reservoir computing
papers.what_it_is: Proves universality of a quantum Wiener reservoir architecture and tests it on reservoir computing benchmarks.

assertions.value: The authors state they give a rigorous proof that qWiener systems retain the fading-memory property and universality of classical Wiener architectures despite quantum constraints.
quotes: We provide the first rigorous proof that qWiener systems retain the fading-memory property and universality of classical Wiener architectures, despite quantum constraints on linear dynamics and measurement back-action.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as proved in the Abstract and Section VI; the theorem number and proof were not checked by this reader.

assertions.value: The authors report that on three benchmark tasks (parity check, NARMA10, delay) their approach consistently outperforms the method in [7]; a classical echo-state network was the baseline.
quotes: We evaluate the simplest qWiener architecture against the model proposed in [7], as well as a classical echo-state network (used as a baseline), on three benchmark reservoir computing tasks: paritycheck, NARMA10, and delay.
Our results demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently outperforms the method in [7].
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation benchmarks from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state it is an open question what advantages the qWiener architecture offers over the classical Wiener architecture, which is also universal.
quotes: In this paper, we have established the universality of the qWiener architecture.
over the classical Wiener architecture, which is also universal.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own statement of scope, Section VI.

papers.what_it_is: A quantum walk based, non-variational algorithm for combinatorial optimisation, tested by numerical simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that numerical simulations on randomly generated instances of five problem types found a globally optimal solution in each case with a small number of iterations.
quotes: weighted maxcut (18 vertices), maximum independent set (18 vertices), kmeans clustering (12 datapoints, 3 clusters), capacitated facility location (12 customers, 3 facility locations), and the quadratic assignment problem (9 locations)
For each problem instance, the algorithm finds a globally optimal solution with a small number of iterations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation of small instances only.

assertions.value: The authors characterise the algorithm as non-variational because, for a given number of iterations, the amplified state is determined by a small set of parameters.
quotes: We characterise the algorithm as non-variational because, given a number of iterations p, the amplified state is determined by a small set of parameters
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' definition, Section V.

assertions.value: The authors state that large-scale benchmarking is future work, so average-case performance and advantage over classical heuristics are not yet shown.
quotes: another important future area of research will involve detailed and large scale benchmarking for various problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' stated limit, Section V.
